content: This document is an updated version of a review originally published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2008. It focuses on comparing laparoscopy and laparotomy for the surgical staging and management of FIGO stage I ovarian cancer. Laparoscopy has become a more commonly used technique for addressing early-stage ovarian tumors, and this review aims to evaluate its advantages and disadvantages compared to the traditional open surgery approach, laparotomy. The objective of this review is to assess the potential benefits and harms of using laparoscopy for the surgical treatment of FIGO stage I ovarian cancer, which includes stages Ia, Ib, and Ic, in comparison to laparotomy. For the original review, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, Biological Abstracts, and CancerLit, covering studies published between January 1, 1990, and November 30, 2007. Additional searches included handsearching relevant journals, reference lists, and conference abstracts. For the first update, the search was extended to include studies up to December 6, 2011, and for this most recent update, the search covered studies published from November 2011 to September 2016. The selection criteria for this review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and prospective cohort studies that compared laparoscopic staging with laparotomy in women diagnosed with FIGO stage I ovarian cancer. However, no studies meeting these criteria were identified. As a result, the review relied on data from non-randomized studies (NRSs) and important findings from other meta-analyses for discussion purposes. No meta-analyses were performed as part of this review. The authors concluded that there is no high-quality evidence available to accurately quantify the risks and benefits of laparoscopy for the management of early-stage ovarian cancer. Therefore, its use as a routine clinical practice cannot be supported or refuted based on the current evidence.
